summary: Sets out privacy and security requirements for DNS-based Service Discovery, which normally reveals information about devices offering and looking for services, such as hostnames and network parameters. That is a concern when mobile devices use it on public networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Looking for a printer by shouting for it in a crowded room tells strangers who you are and what you own. This document lists what is needed to look for nearby services without giving so much away.

questions: what are the privacy requirements for dns service discovery
how can service discovery be made private
subtitle: What privacy and security features DNS-based service discovery needs to protect users on public networks.

tldr.problem: DNS-SD (DNS-based Service Discovery) normally discloses hostnames, device names, and service information to everyone on a network, raising serious privacy concerns when mobile devices use it on public networks like cafes or airports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes privacy and security threats in common service discovery scenarios, cataloging what information gets exposed and deriving a set of requirements for privacy-preserving extensions to DNS-SD.
tldr.outcome: This document provides the requirements that protocol designers need to build privacy-respecting discovery services without sacrificing the usability that makes DNS-SD convenient.

today: RFC 8882 is an informational RFC that provides requirements for future work on privacy-respecting DNS service discovery. The RFC text notes it is a product of the IETF consensus process and was approved for publication, but no standardized privacy-preserving DNS-SD protocol has been issued as a result of this document.

sections.title: The Privacy Problem with Service Discovery
sections.content:
DNS-SD over mDNS (Multicast DNS) enables zero-configuration service discovery in local networks, but it requires public exposure of device identities, hostnames, and service information. This is convenient but creates privacy risks.

Consider a traveler uploading pictures from a phone to a laptop on a cafe's Wi-Fi network. They expect their devices to find each other automatically, but the DNS-SD messages leak information like device names and what services the devices are offering, potentially revealing the traveler's identity to eavesdroppers on the same network.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone shouts out its name and what it is looking for whenever it discovers services. Anyone listening on the network can hear this information.

sections.title: Types of Attackers and Their Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three types of attackers, each with increasing capability. An external attacker is not on the same network link. An on-link attacker is on the same network and can listen to multicast messages. A Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacker can intercept or control network traffic between devices.

All three types can be either passive (just listening) or active (crafting and sending malicious packets). The document focuses on what information passive attackers can learn from DNS-SD messages on the network link.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors can listen from the same network, from outside the network, or by tricking traffic to go through them. The document looks at what each can learn.

sections.title: What Gets Exposed and Why It Matters
sections.content:
DNS-SD publishes three types of records. PTR records associate a service type with an instance name (for example, "Alice's Images . _imageStore._tcp . local"). SRV records provide the hostname, port, priority and weight. TXT records contain attribute-value pairs describing service properties.

Each type leaks sensitive information. Service instance names directly reveal the device owner's identity. Hostnames enable device tracking. TXT records expose service types and software versions, which can be used to fingerprint the device and infer what the user owns. A passive eavesdropper can combine all this information to build a profile of a person's devices and activities.

When a client queries for services, the query itself reveals what the client is looking for, potentially disclosing interests in sensitive services to eavesdroppers.
sections.plainLanguage: The device name says who owns it. The list of services says what gadgets the person has. The service details say what software version they are running. Together, this information can identify a specific person and their devices.

sections.title: What a Privacy-Preserving DNS-SD Needs
sections.content:
For client privacy, DNS-SD messages must avoid disclosure of the client's identity, avoid exposure of linkable identifiers that enable device tracing, and hide the client's interest in specific service types and instances to nodes other than authorized servers.

For private servers (devices that want to be discovered only by authorized clients), messages must avoid disclosing the server's identity or static identifiers like hostnames, must hide service instance names and service attributes from unauthorized clients, and must avoid publishing static IP addresses.

Beyond privacy, a DNS-SD privacy extension must avoid significant CPU overhead that could make nodes vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks, and must not allow small messages to trigger large amounts of traffic toward unverified addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A good discovery system should hide who is looking for what and who is offering what, except to authorized parties. It should also not be easy to break with fake requests.

sections.title: Design Challenges for Privacy Preservation
sections.content:
Several design challenges make privacy preservation difficult. Devices with limited battery power may use proxies to answer discovery queries on their behalf while they sleep, but sharing encryption keys with untrusted proxies is problematic. Hiding service names by randomizing them makes the user interface unusable; users need to know which service to pick.

Secure initialization is needed before devices can trust each other enough to share secrets. Protocol designers can use technologies like passwords, PIN codes, or zero-knowledge proofs, but usability challenges arise when users are tempted to "click OK" without proper verification.

The RFC also notes that lower-layer protections are needed, such as MAC address randomization and link-local addresses, and that metadata about encrypted content can still leak information even if the content itself is protected.
sections.plainLanguage: Making discovery private is hard. Users need to pick the right service from a list, but hiding the names makes that impossible. Also, devices need to trust each other before they can share secrets, but people often skip the security steps to get things working faster.
